ethical coding: Ethical coding means developing software with moral responsibility - considering privacy, accessibility, and societal impact. Good practices include: writing clean, maintainable code; respecting user data; avoiding dark patterns; documenting thoroughly; and ensuring security. Remember, every line of code affects real people!

The ACM Code of Ethics outlines key principles for ethical programming: 1) Contribute to society 2) Avoid harm 3) Be honest 4) Respect privacy 5) Give proper credit 6) Respect intellectual property 7) Consider accessibility 8) Be accountable. Ethical coders ask not just 'can we build this?' but 'should we build this?'

Ethical coding includes writing inclusive software. Consider: color contrast for visually impaired users, keyboard navigation for motor disabilities, alt text for screen readers, and avoiding assumptions about gender/culture. Accessibility isn't optional - it's a fundamental right in our digital world.
white hat hacking: White hat hackers are cybersecurity professionals who use hacking skills ethically to improve security. They perform penetration testing with permission, report vulnerabilities responsibly through bug bounty programs, and help organizations strengthen defenses. Famous examples include finding flaws before criminals do!

Ethical hacking follows strict rules: 1) Get written permission 2) Define scope clearly 3) Report all findings 4) Never exploit for personal gain 5) Respect privacy 6) Help fix vulnerabilities. Many white hats start by practicing on safe environments like Hack The Box or CTF competitions.
responsible disclosure: When finding vulnerabilities, responsible disclosure means: 1) Documenting the issue thoroughly 2) Contacting the vendor privately 3) Giving reasonable time to fix 4) Only publishing details after a patch is available. This balances public safety with giving developers time to address issues properly.

Bug bounty platforms like HackerOne provide structured ways to report vulnerabilities ethically. Top programs pay researchers millions annually for finding flaws in tech giants' systems before criminals can exploit them.
secure coding: Secure coding best practices include: input validation, parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection, proper authentication, principle of least privilege, encryption of sensitive data, and regular dependency updates. OWASP Top 10 lists most critical web app security risks to avoid.

Memory safety is crucial in secure coding. Languages like Rust prevent entire classes of vulnerabilities that plague C/C++. Other safety measures include: bounds checking, sandboxing, and using well-audited cryptographic libraries instead of rolling your own.
ethical ai: Ethical AI development requires: fairness (avoiding biased datasets), transparency (explainable decisions), accountability (clear responsibility), privacy protection, and human oversight. The EU AI Act categorizes systems by risk levels with corresponding requirements.

AI ethics frameworks emphasize: 1) Beneficence (do good) 2) Non-maleficence (do no harm) 3) Autonomy (preserve human choice) 4) Justice (fair distribution of benefits) 5) Explicability (understandable systems).
cybersecurity tips: Essential cybersecurity practices: use strong unique passwords with a manager, enable 2FA everywhere, keep software updated, beware phishing attempts, encrypt sensitive data, back up regularly (3-2-1 rule), and use VPNs on public WiFi.

The CIA triad is cybersecurity's foundation: Confidentiality (data privacy), Integrity (no unauthorized changes), and Availability (reliable access). Good security balances all three without over-emphasizing one at others' expense.
open source ethics: Open source ethics include: proper licensing, giving credit, respecting copyleft requirements, not abusing maintainers' time, and contributing back improvements. Just because code is free doesn't mean it's without obligations or maintainer needs.

Sustainable open source means: funding critical projects, not exploiting volunteer labor, enterprise contributions, and recognizing that most 'free' software relies on someone's unpaid work. Many foundations now help support essential infrastructure.
privacy by design: Privacy by design principles: 1) Proactive not reactive 2) Default privacy settings 3) Privacy embedded into design 4) Full functionality 5) End-to-end security 6) Visibility and transparency 7) Respect for user privacy. GDPR makes this legally required in many cases.

Implementing privacy by design: minimize data collection, anonymize where possible, get explicit consent, allow data access/deletion, encrypt in transit/at rest, and conduct regular privacy impact assessments.
social engineering: Common social engineering attacks: phishing emails, pretexting (fake scenarios), baiting (free malware-infected USBs), quid pro quo (fake tech support), and tailgating (physical access). Defense requires skepticism of unsolicited contacts and verification of identities.

Red team exercises test organizational security by simulating social engineering attacks. Ethical approaches include: getting permission, avoiding real harm, focusing on education, and providing detailed improvement reports.
ethical tech career: Building an ethical tech career: choose employers aligned with your values, speak up about concerns through proper channels, continuously educate yourself on ethics, participate in responsible tech communities, and consider positive-impact projects.

Whistleblowing in tech: last resort after exhausting internal channels, should follow legal protections, requires documented evidence, and often needs lawyer consultation. While risky, ethical disclosures have exposed major privacy violations and safety issues.

port_scanner.description: Basic Python port scanner using sockets to identify open ports
port_scanner.code:
import socket

target = '127.0.0.1'
ports = range(1, 1025)

for port in ports:
    sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_STREAM)
    sock.settimeout(1)
    result = sock.connect_ex((target, port))
    if result == 0:
        print(f'Port {port}: OPEN')
    sock.close()
port_scanner.ethical_use: Only scan systems you own or have permission to test

directory_buster.description: Script to discover hidden directories on web servers
directory_buster.code:
import requests

url = 'http://example.com'
wordlist = ['admin', 'login', 'backup', 'wp-admin']

for word in wordlist:
    full_url = f'{url}/{word}'
    response = requests.get(full_url)
    if response.status_code == 200:
        print(f'Found: {full_url}')

hash_cracker.description: Basic MD5 hash cracker using dictionary attack
hash_cracker.code:
import hashlib

target_hash = '5f4dcc3b5aa765d61d8327deb882cf99'  # 'password'
wordlist = ['password', '123456', 'admin', 'letmein']

for word in wordlist:
    hashed_word = hashlib.md5(word.encode()).hexdigest()
    if hashed_word == target_hash:
        print(f'Found password: {word}')
        break

arp_spoof_detector.description: Detect ARP spoofing attacks on your network
arp_spoof_detector.code:
from scapy.all import sniff, ARP

def detect_arp_spoof(pkt):
    if ARP in pkt and pkt[ARP].op == 2:  # ARP response
        real_mac = get_mac(pkt[ARP].psrc)
        response_mac = pkt[ARP].hwsrc
        if real_mac != response_mac:
            print(f'ARP Spoof detected! {pkt[ARP].psrc} is at {response_mac}')

sniff(prn=detect_arp_spoof, filter='arp', store=0)
